pergunta: How is it possible to add `\printbibliography` to the table of contents (`\tableofcontents`) when using `\usepackage[backend=bibtex,urldate=iso]{biblatex}`?
resposta:
`\printbibliography` only prints the bibliography list. It does **not** automatically create a Table-of-Contents entry. The TOC is built from headings/sections in the document, so you need to either make the bibliography a real section or add a manual TOC line for it.

### Simplest method: manual TOC line
Call `\tableofcontents` early, then before your bibliography use:

```latex
\usepackage[backend=bibtex, urldate=iso]{biblatex}
\begin{document}
\tableofcontents
% ... your text ...

\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Bibliography}
\printbibliography[heading={Bibliography}]

\end{document}
```

Because of multi‑compilation (especially with `backend=bibtex`), run LaTeX **at least twice** (often three times) so the page number of “Bibliography” is corrected.

### Alternative: make it a real section
```latex
\chapter*{Bibliography}
\printbibliography[heading={}]
```

Again, call `\tableofcontents` early and compile a couple of times for correct page numbers.

### If you want individual references in the TOC
Replace bare `\cite{...}` with `\addbibentry{...}`. Biblatex automatically adds those entries to the TOC (unless you globally set `toc=false`):

```latex
According to Smith et al. (2020), ...
\addbibentry{smith2020}
```

The `backend=bibtex` option does **not** affect TOC handling; the same techniques work with any backend. `urldate=iso` only changes how URLs are stored/formatted in the bibliography.

resposta:
**Answer:** Essentially **zero**.

If the ICBM passes **directly overhead** (i.e., its trajectory is vertical or nearly vertical relative to the boat), the point on Earth’s surface directly below it stays fixed — it is just the boat’s location. If the missile instead has horizontal motion (e.g., it sweeps across the sky), its ground track could cover some distance while visible.
